title: UN 38.3, the DG Declaration and 30% State of Charge, by Mode
description: Lithium battery exports run on three proofs: the UN 38.3 test summary, the DG declaration, and state of charge — a 30% legal cap by air, practice by sea.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Lithium-ion battery exports stand on three evidentiary legs: the UN 38.3 test summary that manufacturers and distributors must make available, the dangerous-goods declaration under the modal codes, and state of charge — capped at 30% by law for air shipments, and demanded by carriers and insurers as practice at sea, where the IMDG Code sets no general SoC limit.

title: SCOMET and Lithium Batteries: A Conditional Screen, Not a Ban
description: Ordinary lithium-ion batteries are not SCOMET-controlled: 8A301.e catches bare cells above 350 Wh/kg and exempts batteries. The catch-all is what remains.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: HS 8507.60 lithium-ion batteries are freely exportable and not SCOMET-controlled by default: entry 8A301.e controls bare secondary cells whose energy density exceeds 350 Wh/kg, and its note expressly excludes batteries, including single-cell batteries. What survives for ordinary exporters is the conditional layer — the catch-all obligation of HBP para 10.05 where end-use raises WMD or military-diversion concerns.

title: The Marine Claim File: What the Surveyor Asks For, in Order
description: Marine losses of ₹1 lakh or more need a licensed surveyor by law. The claim file the survey runs on — policy, invoice, B/L, carrier notices — is built earlier.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Indian law routes marine cargo losses of ₹1 lakh or more through a licensed surveyor, and the 2024 Master Circular sets the tempo: surveyor allocated within 24 hours, report within 15 days, decision within 7 days. The surveyor examines a file the exporter built before the loss — policy, invoice, transport documents and the carrier correspondence that preserves recovery.

title: LUT or IGST-Paid: Two Export Routes, Two Failure Chains
description: GST exports run two routes: IGST-paid refunds move through ICEGATE's SB codes; LUT refunds through RFD-01 and deficiency memos. Rule 96B polices both.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Every GST export runs two routes. The IGST-paid route treats the Shipping Bill as the refund application and fails through ICEGATE's SB-series codes; the LUT route refunds unutilised input tax credit through RFD-01 and fails through deficiency memos. Rule 96A adds an export deadline to the LUT, and Rule 96B claws back either refund if proceeds are not realized.

title: General Average for Indian Shippers: Bonds, Guarantees and the COI
description: When general average is declared, cargo is released against security: a GA bond plus an insurer's guarantee — or a cash deposit if the cargo sailed uninsured.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: General average makes every cargo owner on a voyage pay a share of sacrifices made to save it, and the ship releases cargo only against security: a general average bond from the receiver plus either a cash deposit or a guarantee from the cargo insurer. For insured cargo the COI does the paying; uninsured cargo posts the deposit itself.

title: Export Realization in 2026: EDPMS, e-BRC and a Clock That Moved Twice
description: India's export-realization period moved twice in seven months — 9 to 15 and back to 9 — and new FEMA regulations take force 1 October 2026. The date decides.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: An Indian exporter's realization deadline now depends on the shipment date: nine months for exports before 14 November 2025, fifteen months for shipments up to 4 June 2026, nine months again since, and fifteen or eighteen months once the 2026 FEMA export regulations take force on 1 October 2026. EDPMS tracks every bill against that clock.

title: EDPMS Open Entries and Caution-Listing: How Exporters Get Flagged
description: Caution-listing stopped being automatic in 2020: AD banks recommend it on adverse notice or evasion. From October 2026, one year overdue means advance-or-LC.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Caution-listing stopped being automatic in October 2020: the AD bank recommends it to RBI on adverse agency notice (ED, CBI, DRI), untraceability, or lack of sincere realization efforts. A listed exporter ships only against advance payment or irrevocable LC — and from 1 October 2026, Regulation 13 applies that consequence mechanically at one year past due.

title: e-BRC Self-Certification: From Bank Realization to Refund Document
description: Since 15 November 2023, exporters self-generate e-BRCs on the DGFT portal from bank-uploaded IRMs. Purpose codes gate what qualifies; matching keys decide it.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The electronic Bank Realization Certificate moved to self-certification on 15 November 2023: banks upload inward remittance messages to the DGFT portal, and the exporter generates e-BRCs by mapping IRMs to shipping bills. Purpose codes gate eligibility, four matching keys decide the linkage, and the resulting certificate feeds GST refunds and incentive returns.

title: AD Code Registration on ICEGATE: The Gate Before the Scroll
description: AD Code registration went port-agnostic in June 2022, but bank accounts still register per port for refunds — and PFMS validates before any money moves.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The Authorised Dealer Code links every Shipping Bill to the exporter's bank, and its registration mechanics changed materially: since June 2022, an AD Code registered at one port applies at all customs locations, while bank-account registration for refunds remains per-port. CBIC standardised the paperwork to two documents in 2023 — and PFMS validates the account before any disbursal.

title: Reviewer-of-record
description: The reviewer-of-record is the named human who examines and signs every evidence packet — identity, timestamp, override log and hash — before it is relied on.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The reviewer-of-record is the named human professional who examines an evidence packet and signs it before anyone relies on it. The signature is structural: the packet carries the reviewer's identity, timestamp, a log of every override made, and a sign-off hash — so accountability for machine-assisted work lands on a person, permanently and inspectably.

title: Four-state readiness
description: Four-state readiness grades every checked field OPEN, BLOCKED, CONDITIONAL or UNCLEAR — a verdict system where missing evidence can never silently pass.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Four-state readiness is TradeWatch's verdict system: every checked field on a shipment resolves to exactly one of OPEN, BLOCKED, CONDITIONAL or UNCLEAR. The fourth state is the architectural point — missing or ambiguous evidence is surfaced as UNCLEAR rather than defaulted to a pass, so silence can never impersonate compliance.

title: Validated-at-source vs Inferred: Two Ways to Know a Supply Chain
description: Supply-chain intelligence splits into two kinds: inferred models built from external signals, and validated-at-source records built from the shipment itself.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Supply-chain knowledge comes in two epistemically different kinds. Inferred intelligence reconstructs a chain from the outside — trade statistics, manifests, news, graphs of probabilistic links. Validated-at-source intelligence is built from the shipment's own documents, checked against primary rules, and signed. The two differ not in degree but in what a user may safely do with them.

title: SCMTR Goes Fully Live: India's Manifest Regime After 30 June 2026
description: SCMTR's transitional phase ended: after extensions to 31 March and then 30 June 2026, CBIC's circular of 1 July 2026 implements the manifest regime pan-India.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The Sea Cargo Manifest and Transhipment Regulations, 2018 finished their seven-year transition in mid-2026. After extensions to 31 March and then 30 June 2026, CBIC's circular of 1 July 2026 implements SCMTR pan-India: all messages except import transhipment are fully operational, with penal action for technical difficulties held back until 31 August 2026.

title: India's New Sea-Carriage Statutes: CGSA 2025 and Bills of Lading Act
description: On 10 September 2025 India replaced its 1925 carriage act and 1856 bills of lading act in one stroke — Acts 18 and 19 of 2025, commenced by twin notifications.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: India's sea-carriage statute book turned over on one day: the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 both came into force on 10 September 2025, repealing the 1925 carriage act and the 1856 bills of lading act. Substance is preserved — Hague-Visby rules, transfer of suit rights — but every citation changed.

title: eCoO 2.0: India's Certificates of Origin Went Fully Electronic
description: Non-preferential CoOs went e-only on 1 January 2025 and preferential on 17 January via eCoO 2.0 — with back-to-back CoOs, a ₹200 fee and 125 issuing agencies.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: India's Certificates of Origin moved fully online in January 2025: DGFT made electronic filing of non-preferential CoOs mandatory from 1 January and preferential CoOs from 17 January on the eCoO 2.0 platform. The same reform introduced online back-to-back non-preferential CoOs, a ₹200 per-certificate fee, and one platform across 125 issuing agencies.

title: Subrogation Time-Bars: CGSA 2025's One Year, MTGA 1993's Nine Months
description: Cargo suits die by statute: one year under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025, nine months under MTGA 1993. Expiry extinguishes claim and subrogation.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: India's cargo-claim clocks extinguish rights rather than merely bar remedies: suit against a sea carrier within one year of delivery under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025, and against a multimodal transport operator within nine months under MTGA 1993. Once expired, the insurer's subrogation target is gone, and the cargo claim usually follows.

title: Open Cover vs Certificate of Insurance: Reconciling CIF+10%
description: A Certificate of Insurance draws on the open cover only if declared, in time, at 110% of CIF. Under-insurance leaves the assured his own insurer for the gap.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: An open cover insures only what is declared into it, and a Certificate of Insurance is only as good as its declared value. UCP 600 Article 28(f)(ii) sets the floor at 110% of CIF; Section 81 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 makes the under-insured assured his own insurer for the shortfall; Section 64VB governs attachment.

title: Marine Cargo Claim Denial in India: A Taxonomy of Evidence Gaps
description: Marine cargo claims in India fail on evidence, not perils: Section 64VB premium timing, packing exclusions, notice windows and expired time-bars decide them.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Marine cargo claim denials in India cluster into four evidence families, not exotic perils: premium timing under Section 64VB of the Insurance Act 1938, policy exclusions such as ICC clause 4.3 on packing, procedural windows for notice and suit, and cross-document inconsistency across the invoice, packing list, B/L and Certificate of Insurance. Every family is checkable before sailing.

title: LC First Presentations: Why Seven in Ten Fail on Documents
description: ICC surveys found ~70% of LC presentations rejected first time. UCP 600 gives banks five days and one refusal notice; the fixable causes are documentary.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The ICC's own introduction to UCP 600 records that roughly 70% of letter-of-credit presentations were rejected on first presentation. The examination rules are mechanical: banks get five banking days, transport documents must be presented within 21 calendar days of shipment, the invoice description must correspond with the credit, and refusal comes as a single notice listing every discrepancy.

title: HS Classification Drift Across the Invoice, Shipping Bill and COO
description: HS codes drift across the invoice, Shipping Bill and Certificate of Origin — one digit shifts duty, RoDTEP rate and origin claims. Shipping Bills need 8 digits.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The same goods routinely carry different HS codes on the commercial invoice, the Shipping Bill and the Certificate of Origin, because each document is produced from a different master. The Shipping Bill demands the full eight-digit ITC(HS) item, RoDTEP rates diverge line by line at eight digits, and CAROTAR 2020 makes origin claims turn on classification-linked criteria.

title: EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542: The HS 8507.60 Compliance Calendar
description: EU Battery Regulation dates for HS 8507.60 exporters: CE and importer checks bind now, the passport lands 18.02.2027, due diligence moved to 18.08.2027.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: The EU Battery Regulation binds Indian HS 8507.60 exporters through their importers today — CE marking, declaration of conformity, technical documentation per Article 41 — while its headline obligations arrive on staggered dates: the battery passport on 18 February 2027, due diligence on 18 August 2027, and the EV carbon-footprint declaration only once its delegated act is finally adopted.

title: e-SANCHIT: The Upload Failures That Stall Assessment and LEO
description: e-SANCHIT rejects uploads that break its spec — PDF/A, 200 dpi, 75 KB per page, signed with the ICEGATE-registered DSC. A failed IRN stalls assessment and LEO.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: e-SANCHIT is the only channel for supporting documents on ICEGATE, and it enforces a precise technical specification: PDF/A (ISO 19005-2), at least 200 dpi, 75 KB per A4 page within a 1 MB file, digitally signed with the DSC registered on ICEGATE. A defective upload yields no IRN, and without the IRN the document does not exist for assessment.

title: What One Documentation Failure Costs: Demurrage, Fees, Blocked Refunds
description: One export document error rarely bills you once: container rent climbs by slab, banks charge USD 100 per discrepant set, and the refund clock stops until fixed.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: A single documentation failure bills an exporter through four independent meters: container charges that escalate by slab at the terminal, bank discrepancy fees per presentation, fixed rectification fees at customs, and a refund clock that legally stops until the error is cured. The instruments are published — the anatomy is simply rarely added up.

title: US Tariffs on Indian Exports 2026: From 50% to 10%, and the July Cliff
description: US tariffs on Indian goods fell from 50% to a 10% surcharge in five steps — a trade deal, a Supreme Court ruling, and a Section 122 clock expiring 24 July 2026.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Between August 2025 and July 2026, the US tariff on Indian-origin goods moved from a stacked 50% to a 10% surcharge, through a trade framework, an Executive Order, and a Supreme Court ruling that voided the IEEPA tariffs. The Section 122 surcharge expires by statute on 24 July 2026; Section 232 duties on metals and autos stack separately and remain.

title: CBAM's Definitive Regime: What EU Buyers Now Ask Indian Suppliers
description: CBAM's definitive regime began 1 January 2026: EU importers of steel and aluminium goods over 50 tonnes a year need authorisation, emissions data, certificates.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: CBAM's definitive regime took effect on 1 January 2026. EU importers of covered iron, steel and aluminium goods above the new 50-tonne annual threshold must be authorised CBAM declarants, and their first declaration — due 30 September 2027 for 2026 imports — prices embedded emissions with certificates. The data burden lands upstream, on the Indian producer.

title: SB005: Why Your IGST Refund Blocks After EGM and How to Clear It
description: SB005 blocks an IGST refund when the Shipping Bill invoice number diverges from GSTR-1 Table 6A. The fix is a Concordance Table filed with the customs officer.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: An SB005 error blocks an IGST refund when the Shipping Bill invoice number diverges from the one filed in GSTR-1 Table 6A. The refund stalls silently after EGM; no rejection is issued. The fix is a Concordance Table (Annexure A) verified through the customs officer interface at ₹1,000 per Shipping Bill — the Shipping Bill itself cannot be amended.

title: Reconciling Invoice, Packing List, B/L and Shipping Bill Before LEO
description: Invoice, packing list, B/L and Shipping Bill must agree field by field before LEO. Section 149 of the Customs Act bars most amendments once goods are exported.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Four documents describe one shipment — Commercial Invoice, Packing List, Bill of Lading and Shipping Bill — and customs, GST and manifest systems check them against each other after export, once Section 149 of the Customs Act has frozen the declaration. Pre-LEO reconciliation verifies identity, quantity, value and cargo fields for agreement while every record is still writable.

title: Invoice Number Formatting: How Tally and ICEGATE Disagree
description: Rule 46(b) allows 16 characters and only hyphen and slash in a GST invoice number. Formats that drift between Tally, GSTR-1 and the Shipping Bill trigger SB005.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: Rule 46(b) of the CGST Rules limits a tax invoice number to sixteen characters from letters, numerals, hyphen and slash. Accounting-software formats and the Shipping Bill entry routinely diverge — a dropped prefix, a slash swapped for a hyphen — and ICES matches invoice numbers exactly, so any divergence returns SB005 and stalls the IGST refund.

title: SB001–SB006: The ICEGATE Shipping Bill Error Codes, Explained
description: SB001–SB006 are ICES validation codes for IGST export refunds. Each code names one mismatch between GSTR-1, the Shipping Bill and the EGM — each with one fix.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: ICES validates every IGST export refund at invoice level against GSTR-1 data and returns one of seven codes, SB000 through SB006. Each error code names a specific mismatch — Shipping Bill details, EGM status, GSTIN or invoice number — and each has a fixing actor and procedure. Even SB000 does not always pay: four conditions gate the refund scroll.

title: RoDTEP 2026: The February Cut, the March Restoration, the Fine Print
description: DGFT halved RoDTEP rates on 23 February 2026 and restored them from 23 March. A corrigendum kept the cut in force for shipments in the intervening month.
author: Sreenath Govindarajan
summary: DGFT Notification 60/2025-26 cut all RoDTEP rates and value caps by 50% with effect from 23 February 2026. Notification 66/2025-26 restored the 22 February rates from 23 March 2026 — and its corrigendum confirmed the restoration is not retroactive, so exports with LEO between 23 February and 22 March 2026 (outside ITC HS Chapters 01–24) retain the halved rates.
